```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

# Keep data.table within CRAN's thread limits
data.table::setDTthreads(2)
```

```{r load}
library(WSSmod)
```

WSSmod ships files in `inst/extdata` that belong to a named *prebuilt
reference set*, plus two small simulated datasets for examples. This vignette
describes each one: what it is, how to load it, and what it can and cannot be
used for. The other vignettes put them to use:
[Calculating Weighted Sum Scores](calculating-wss.html) and
[Predicting Weighted Sum Scores from plasma biomarkers](predicting-wss.html).

## Available reference sets

```{r list}
list_prebuilt_wss()
```

There is one set, `"core_AD_plasma_biomarkers"`. Every function below takes it
as its `prebuilt` argument, and as the default. A set can have up to four
files, and each is read with its own function:

| File | Function | Contents |
|------|----------|----------|
| scores | `load_prebuilt_wss()` | module and protein weighting table |
| terms | `wss_prebuilt_terms()` | module labels and enrichment summary |
| model | `load_prebuilt_wss_model()` | fitted `joinet` prediction model |
| biomarker reference | `load_prebuilt_biomarker_reference()` | anonymized baseline biomarker values |

## The module and protein weighting table

`load_prebuilt_wss()` returns the table that `calculate_WSS()` uses by default,
with one row per protein-in-module assignment.

```{r scores}
weights <- load_prebuilt_wss()
dim(weights)
names(weights)
```

The columns `calculate_WSS()` needs are

* `module`: module name, built as `Biomarker`, a dot, and `cluster`
  (for example `Merged.M17`),
* `symbol`: protein gene symbol, matching the columns of your matrix,
* `mean_beta`: its sign sets the direction a protein is aligned in,
* `mean_alpha_scaled`: the weight of the protein within its module, scaled to
  at most 1.

```{r scores-head}
head(weights[, c("module", "symbol", "term", "mean_beta", "mean_alpha_scaled")])
```

The other columns describe where a row came from: the identifiers `GENE` and
`ix` (an aptamer identifier), the module's `term` label, the original
biomarker-specific groups and terms that the protein came from (`orig_groups`
and `orig_terms`), and network connectivity summaries (`mean_degree` and
`mean_strength`).

### Why a protein can be in several modules

A protein can be assigned to more than one module, because the modules were
built from several biomarker analyses and then merged.

```{r duplicates}
c(
  rows = nrow(weights),
  proteins = length(unique(weights$symbol)),
  modules = length(unique(weights$module))
)

# Proteins that are in more than one module
multi <- weights[, .N, by = symbol][N > 1]
nrow(multi)
weights[symbol == multi$symbol[1], c("module", "symbol", "term", "mean_alpha_scaled")]
```

`calculate_WSS()` removes this overlap before scoring. It keeps each protein
in the module where it has the highest `mean_alpha_scaled` (the `dedup_by`
argument), then drops modules with fewer than `min_module_size` proteins (3 by
default). That leaves the 75 modules that the prediction model also covers.

```{r dedup}
res <- calculate_WSS(wss_example_expression)
c(
  modules_scored = ncol(res$scores),
  proteins_scored = length(unique(unlist(res$module_proteins)))
)
```

## Module term labels

`wss_prebuilt_terms()` returns one row per scored module with a short label,
the group the module came from, and `mean.Zsum`, the Zsummary preservation
score of the module across 12 independent GNPC cohorts in the
[preprint](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.08.14.26360394v1.full-text).

```{r terms}
terms <- wss_prebuilt_terms()
dim(terms)
head(terms)
```

The `name` column matches the module names in the weighting table and in the
columns of `calculate_WSS()` and `predict_WSS()` results, so it can be used to
label them:

```{r terms-match}
modules <- colnames(res$scores)[1:3]
terms$term[match(modules, terms$name)]
```

`group` is the biomarker analysis a module came from, with `Merged` for modules
built from all of them together.

```{r terms-group}
table(terms$group)
```

## The prediction model

`load_prebuilt_wss_model()` returns a list with the fitted model and what it
needs.

```{r model}
model_info <- load_prebuilt_wss_model()
names(model_info)
model_info$variant
model_info$x_cols
head(model_info$outcomes)
length(model_info$outcomes)
```

* `x_cols` are the predictor columns `predict_WSS()` requires, in order: age,
  sex and the eight plasma biomarkers.
* `outcomes` are the 75 module names it predicts, the same names as in the
  terms table.
* `variant` names the set of predictors the model was trained on.
* `model` is the fitted `joinet` object. Predicting from it needs the suggested
  packages `glmnet` and `joinet`, which is why the other vignette guards those
  chunks. Reading the list does not need them, so nothing above does.

To predict, use `predict_WSS()` rather than the model directly.

## The anonymized biomarker reference

`load_prebuilt_biomarker_reference()` returns baseline values for the eight
plasma biomarkers, in long format, that `normalize_wss_biomarkers()` uses with
`method = "project"`.

```{r reference}
reference <- load_prebuilt_biomarker_reference()
head(reference, 3)
reference[, .(n = .N, median = signif(median(value), 3)), by = biomarker]
```

This reference data comes from real distributions, but each biomarker has been 
scrambled independently to completely anonymize the values. It is used only for
per-biomarker questions, such as where a new value falls within the
distribution. It has no valid joint structure, so do not use it to look at
relationships between biomarkers or to train or evaluate models.

## Simulated example data

Two datasets, available as soon as the package is loaded, are simulated and have no biological
meaning. They exist for examples and tests:

* `wss_example_expression`: a 50-sample by 887-protein matrix covering every
  protein in the default modules,
* `wss_example_biomarkers`: age, sex and eight raw biomarkers for 20 patients.

```{r simulated}
dim(wss_example_expression)
dim(wss_example_biomarkers)
```

## Provenance and use

The prebuilt files were derived from plasma proteomic and biomarker data from
the Longo Lab, as described in the [preprint](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.08.14.26360394v1.full-text). They are included so that scores can be calculated and predicted
without access to the original data.

## Adding a reference set

Reference sets are listed in one registry in the package source,
`.wss_prebuilt_registry` in `R/prebuilt_wss.R`. A new set is registered by
giving it a name and the file names of its parts. Only the scores file is
required; the terms, model and biomarker reference files are optional, and the
loaders return `NULL` for a part a set does not have. The files go in
`inst/extdata`, and the new name then appears in `list_prebuilt_wss()`.
